items.title: She Tried to Live as a Man Before Detransitioning. Now, Her Story Is Part of a Powerful Book and Podcast Series
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Author Paul Hastings is on a mission to share powerful stories about “ordinary people” inspired by an “extraordinary God.”

In fact, that’s part of the title of his book, “Compelled: Ordinary People Extraordinary God,” a project that shares incredible testimonies of people who have gone from darkness to light, have faced difficult circumstances — and found freedom.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Hastings, who hosts a podcast by the same name, said his mission to tell such powerful stories developed after years of working full-time in politics.

“I got really burned out, as you could imagine, just like the political cycle always, always on,” he said. “And so my wife and I just began praying like, ‘Lord, there are other things that you know I could do.’ And one thing that I was convicted about is that the whole time that I was in the political sphere, I had never once stopped to pray for my political opponents. I just cared about their personal destruction, which just sounds terrible, but I’m just being honest.”

This conviction led Hastings deeper into prayer, and he reflected on how God can change any heart, regardless of how terrible a person has behaved. This became the root of the “Compelled” podcast. The book simply builds upon that effort.

“The whole premise of the podcast, the radio show, and the book ‘Compelled’ is to find people with these amazing stories that their life truly exemplifies what it means to live a life compelled by Christ,” Hastings said. “So stories of stark transformation.”

He had to narrow over 100 stories down to just seven for the book, including everything from people who have been missionaries to cannibal tribes in Papua New Guinea to a mom who was falsely accused of murder and sentenced to life in prison.

“Each of these people has an amazing testimony … Christ just radically transformed who they are and how they lived,” Hastings said. “And trying to choose the top seven to place into our book was not an easy feat. That was probably one of the hardest tasks about the book, but hopefully we did a good job.”

Hastings said one of the stories that most stuck with him was Laura Perry Smalts, a woman who previously identified as transgender and lived for years as a man before finding Christ.

“When she was in her early 20s, she made a decision to reject everything that she’d ever been taught,” he said. “She thought that she would find answers by transgendering herself into a man. And so over the course of 10 years, she surgically removed every female organ from her body.”

Ultimately, after altering her body, going on testosterone, and growing a beard while living as an individual named “Jake,” Smalts changed her heart and mind.

“Today, Laura lives a completely different life than the one that she once lived,” he said, noting she has shared her testimony. “And it’s just an incredible testimony of the Lord’s goodness and kindness that no one is too far gone, that the Lord can save anybody in any type of circumstance.”

Ultimately, Hastings said he wants people to know it’s never too late to change.

“The Lord can save anybody,” he said. “So if you’ve got an aunt, an uncle, a child, and a cousin, a friend, a neighbor, and you think to yourself, ‘Man, this person is too far gone. They’re too far lost. They cannot be redeemed.’ That’s not true. … The Lord can take the most hardened sinner and transform their life.”

items.title: Do Prophets Still Exist? Meet the Filmmaker Who’s Investigating This Biblical Phenomenon
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Interesting.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Filmmaker Matthew Thayer is on a mission to explore whether modern-day prophets are still delivering important messages.

Thayer’s new film, “Can You Hear Me Now?” tackles this timeless topic, exploring whether the biblical dynamic of prophets delivering God’s Word to humanity is still alive and active today.

The film director said he “absolutely” believes God still speaks through prophets, explaining his perspective that individuals with this ability happened to “just kind of show up in the Bible.”

“There’s nothing that actually says, ‘Oh, this is what a prophet is,’ and so what that means to me is that the ancient Middle East — they were just there,” Thayer said of biblical prophets. “So the people of that era and the people that were originally receiving the words of the Bible originally just understood what a prophet was and a prophet’s function.”

The director believes it’s been proven that people have had dreams and experiences they can’t explain — sequences that tell them what will happen; Thayer said these are often quite accurate. He believes that’s because God has enabled them, through Him, to witness elements of the unseen realm.

When asked why some people in the church world might dismiss modern-day prophecy, Thayer held little back.

“Honestly, I think it’s because the dark spiritual forces that we war against, according to Ephesians 6, knew that communications with God was the first thing that they needed to take out,” he said. “Communications are taken out in warfare first … that’s just a standard warfare practice, and, so, if we are actually in a spiritual war, it would make sense that they would target prophets first.”

Thayer advocated being careful about the sources people gather their prophecy from, as false prophets can open people up to deception. Thus, discernment is key.

“To me, it’s more about who the prophet is pointing to,” he said. “Because that’s what Deuteronomy 13 very clearly stipulates … that there’s going to be false prophets and they’re going to be accurate. But if they’re pointing you away from Yahweh, if they’re pointing you away from God, then they’re a false prophet.”

Thayer understands some of the hesitation people have surrounding prophecy, explaining that his own skepticism came when politics and prophecy collided. He said it felt like some of those making proclamations — especially surrounding President Donald Trump in 2016 — felt like they didn’t quite land. But, over time, the volume of so-called “words” surrounding Trump shocked him.

“The amount of words that were coming out just kind of made me go, like, ‘I think God’s actually trying to do something,'” he said. “He’s trying to alert people to what’s going on and so that’s kind of one of the things that I was exploring with the documentary.”

Thayer recalled being in an auditorium in 2007, when faith leader Kim Clement offered up a prophecy many saw as predicting Trump’s presidency.

“We’re all standing there going like, ‘What? Like the apprentice guy? What?'” Thayer recalled, noting how Clement said Trump would be a trumpet. “Well, what does a trumpet do? A trumpet calls to attention, a trumpet calls people to action, and that’s actually really kind of very close to what [Trump’s] doing — like he’s pointing at things that we didn’t even know existed, and darkness, and corruption that was happening within our government.”

items.title: After Eight Years, ‘The Chosen’ Has Filmed Its Final Scene
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: For eight years there was always another day of shooting The Chosen on the calendar. Now there isn’t. The series about the life of Jesus has wrapped filming on its seventh and final season in Midlothian, Texas, finishing a shoot that started in late April, according to The Dallas Morning News, which
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

For eight years there was always another day of shooting The Chosen on the calendar. Now there isn’t.

The series about the life of Jesus has wrapped filming on its seventh and final season in Midlothian, Texas, finishing a shoot that started in late April, according to The Dallas Morning News, which toured the set with other Texas outlets on Sept. 21.

Season 7 covers the Resurrection. Season 6, the Crucifixion, starts streaming on Prime Video Nov. 15, and a theatrical version of the Crucifixion arrives March 12, 2027.

The show has been filming at Camp Hoblitzelle, a 1,200-acre property south of Dallas, since Season 3, on a set that includes a full replica of Capernaum. Creator Dallas Jenkins moved his family to Midlothian to be close to it. What started as a crowdfunded pilot with no distribution has grown into a series that 5&2 Studios says has reached more than 300 million viewers worldwide.

“When we were on our first day on set, we didn’t know anyone was going to be watching,” Jenkins told reporters in a Q&A published by The Dallas Morning News. “We had no idea what the future held. We were just a small group of artists trying to make something work. Now, eight years later, we’re still doing that, even though we have a bigger crew, even though we have more toys to play with, even though now there’s hundreds of millions of people watching.”

The Resurrection was the part he’d been nervous about. For the first few seasons, he said, he steered away from the supernatural because it’s “a hard thing to capture and do right” and he wasn’t sure the show had the tools.

“In this season, I’ve had to give up some of that,” he said. “There’s some supernatural things that happen in Season 6 and 7 that have to be captured.”

Asked what eight years of filming the Gospels did to his own faith, Jenkins pointed to one thing: “The thing that has stood out the most is how intimate Jesus was with people. I believe that this show has taught me, and it seems to have engaged viewers in the same way, that Jesus wants a personal relationship with you.”

Jenkins posted a video from the wrap party on Saturday with a caption that reads like someone who just put down a very large backpack: “For the first time, I don’t have another day of filming The Chosen hanging over my head. And one word keeps coming to mind.”

The word is gratitude.

“My eyes are a little teary from the crying I’ve been doing tonight,” he says in the video, standing outside the party after what he counts as 528 days of filming. “But my immense gratitude, that’s the word that just keeps going over and over through my head. And I want to make sure you hear me who I’m most grateful to first. And that’s God, who birthed this project through me. And I’ll never fully understand why he chose me to do it.”

He remembers the morning of the last shoot day. “I woke up and I had so much joy in my heart for the first time in 528 days of filming,” he says. “I just went into the front lawn doing kind of my morning prayer and alone time, and I just kept saying to God, look what you’ve done. Look at what you’ve done.”

He thanks his wife, Amanda, who went through cancer during the run of the show, his kids, the cast and crew, and the viewers who crowdfunded it. “We are not financed by a major studio,” he says. “I can’t thank you enough for that.”

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Dallas Jenkins (@dallas.jenkins)

The Chosen is finished filming, but Jenkins isn’t finished with biblical epics. A Joseph of Egypt miniseries the team shot last year is due early next year, a Moses show goes into a writers’ retreat in November and an animated project called Chosen Adventures is underway. He told reporters the Book of Acts is the long-term plan.

“I love this cast and crew, but we’re going to take a little break for a bit,” he said. “We’ll come back hopefully in a few years to do Acts.”

items.title: Different Eyes: The Catholic Demon and the X-Men
items.author: Matthew Malone
items.summary:
Matthew Malone

Beneath Nightcrawler’s fierce exterior is a character of Christian faith who inspires those around him to see the world through “different eyes.”
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Matthew Malone

X-Men is one of the most iconic and enduring comics of all time. The series was created by the legendary Stan Lee and Jack Kirby for Marvel Comics and has become a major cultural force in the modern era, spawning countless comic book spin-offs, animated television series, and film franchises. Yet behind the colorful costumes, extraordinary powers, and weird and wonderful characters lies a sustained exploration into prejudice, alienation, identity, friendship, and faith. One of the franchise’s most fascinating characters is Kurt Wagner, the blue-skinned, demonic-looking mutant known as Nightcrawler. Beneath his fierce exterior is a character of Christian faith who inspires those around him to see the world through “different eyes”—a paradox that places him at the heart of the X-Men’s most enduring questions about humanity, otherness, suffering and the nature of the soul. 

Stan Lee created the X-Men in 1963. Rather than creating individual origin stories, Lee conceived of mutants—individuals born with genetic mutations that gave them extraordinary powers. Nightcrawler was created by artist Dave Cockrum and debuted in Giant-size X-Men #1 (1975). Nightcrawler, or Kurt Wagner, is blue-skinned with yellow eyes, pointed ears, long fangs, a prehensile tail, and the power of teleportation. Unlike characters like Rogue or even Wolverine, who could conceal their mutant powers from human society, Nightcrawler cannot hide his appearance. He is forced to confront the fear and prejudice of humanity in a direct and personal way. Yet he never retreats into hatred or bitterness against his persecutors; rather, he responds with compassion, humility, and forgiveness, guided by his Catholic convictions. 

Nightcrawler’s faith thereby provides a striking contrast to his outward appearance and his swashbuckling, musketeer-like persona. Writer Chris Claremont recognized something paradoxical at the heart of Kurt Wagner:

For all his extreme physiognomy, he’s one of the most human and decent members of the team. In many ways, he’s the emotional/spiritual center of the group.

In this respect, the character recalls Victor Hugo’s The Hunchback of Notre Dame (1831) or David Lynch’s depiction of Joseph Merrick in The Elephant Man (1980). Like Quasimodo and Merrick, Nightcrawler challenges society’s tendencies to judge based on outward appearances; what appears monstrous does not diminish the God-given dignity of the person, and beneath a frightening exterior may be extraordinary beauty. 

The story of Kurt Wagner is one of abandonment, ostracization, and courage in the face of prejudice—perhaps best remembered in the X-Men Animated Series, season 3, episode 18 (1995). The episode’s writer, Len Uhley, described it in his estimation as “the first mainstream cartoon that dealt with issues of faith.” 

The episode follows Rogue, Gambit, and Wolverine as they travel to the Bavarian Alps, where reports of a “demon” lead them to a Catholic monastery. Wolverine tracks the creature and discovers Kurt Wagner (Nightcrawler). The episode explores Kurt’s tragic past: Abandoned by his mother, Mystique, he is forced to perform as a freakish acrobatic attraction in a traveling circus before fleeing and discovering refuge in the monastery. He finds solace in the community of Catholic monks who judge him not according to his appearance but the beauty of his heart. This provides the foundation for one of the most remarkable explorations of faith in the history of comic book animated television. Wolverine—a cynical, violent, and traumatized anti-hero whose suffering and anger has driven him away from God—confronts Nightcrawler about his Catholic faith, resulting in a remarkable dialogue: 

Nightcrawler: Though all people are flawed and struggle with the capacity for sin, none like to be reminded of our shared human weakness. My appearance does not make it easy. 

Wolverine: Doesn’t it make you crazy? 

Nightcrawler: It did once, but then I found peace by devoting my life to God. He directed me to this place where they value the character of my heart, not my appearance. 

Wolverine: What are you talking about? God gave up on us long ago! 

Nightcrawler: No, my friend, God does not give up on his children—human or mutant. He is there for us in our times of joy and to help us when we are in pain—if we let Him. . . . We are alike, you and I—angry at the world. My pain drives me to seek God, yours drove you away. 

Wolverine (pops his claws out): Don’t tell me about God! What kind of God would let men do this to me? 

Nightcrawler: Our ability to understand God’s purpose is limited. But we take comfort in the fact that His love is limitless! 

Wolverine (sheathes claws): I used to buy into all of that. But I’ve lived too long and done too much. 

Nightcrawler: Life will always be hard. I understand this better than most. Yet, despite it all, people of every faith believe there is a God who loves them. Can so many be wrong? Open your heart, Logan. Would it hurt so much to see the world through different eyes? 

This dialogue shows the stark contrast between the two characters. Wolverine is unable to reconcile his pain with the existence of a loving and omnipotent God. However, Nightcrawler recognizes that Wolverine’s doubt and cynicism is rooted not simply in intellectual doubt but in lived suffering.

Wolverine’s position recalls the classic formulation of the problem of evil articulated by St. Thomas Aquinas in his Summa theologiae: 

If, therefore, God existed, there would be no evil discoverable; but there is evil in the world. Therefore God does not exist. 

Nightcrawler’s response finds a striking parallel in Aquinas’s answer to this objection, which draws from St. Augustine: 

Since God is the highest good, He would not allow any evil to exist in His works, unless His omnipotence and goodness were such as to bring good even out of evil. 

Rather than judging Wolverine, Nightcrawler responds with pastoral compassion and understanding. He invites his newly found friend to see with “different eyes” beyond his own pain to recognize that he is a part of God’s broader human family. The exchange presents two radically different responses to suffering, pain, and loneliness; Wolverine’s pain drives him to anger and isolation, while Nightcrawler’s brings him closer to God. 

As the episode progresses, one of the monks betrays Nightcrawler and informs the townspeople that a “demon” is living in the monastery. The villagers arrive with pitchforks, blades, and fiery torches. In the fury and chaos, the mob sets the monastery ablaze. Nightcrawler confronts the monk who betrayed him, and rather than seeking revenge, he responds in a Christlike manner with forgiveness and understanding: 

It is not for me to judge you, Brother Reinhardt, the question is how will God judge you? Look around you, this is the fruit of your labors, not mine. 

It is at this moment that Wolverine begins to see the power of Nightcrawler’s faith. As the monastery’s embers smoke and rise in the sky, Nightcrawler hands Wolverine a Bible, culminating in an extraordinarily profound exchange: 

Nightcrawler: Thank you, my friends. Your presence here was a great blessing.

Wolverine: What do you mean, blessing? Look at this place! We blew it! 

Nightcrawler: I disagree with you. Brother Reinhard understands his tragic mistake and has repented. The townspeople no longer look at me with fear in their hearts. There was no loss of life. All are reasons to be thankful.

Rogue: What about the monastery? 

Nightcrawler: A great tragedy. But it was only stone and mortar. The foundation God has built in our hearts can never be destroyed. 

Wolverine: Man, I don’t get you. 

Nightcrawler (hands Wolverine a Bible): Here, I’ve marked a few passages you may find rewarding. Remember, Logan, “different eyes.” 

The episode’s conclusion echoes the Augustinian principle outlined by Aquinas: Something good can come from evil. In this case, the good culminates in Rogue finding Wolverine alone in a Catholic church. Wolverine is praying and reading from Nightcrawler’s Bible, intoning the words from Isaiah 12:1, “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, for though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, and you comforted me.”

This is a remarkable moment in comic book and animated television history. X-Men: The Animated Series (1992-1997) reached an enormous audience of children and young adults and has since experienced renewed interest through the contemporary reboot X-Men ’97. Here was a mainstream animated series in which a Catholic character spoke openly about God and forgiveness, inspiring its archetypal violent, cynical, and rebellious anti-hero to pray and contemplate redemption—all within a single twenty-minute episode. 

Nightcrawler’s Catholicism has remained one of the defining aspects of his character. Throughout his long tenure in the X-Men series, he has consistently been depicted as one of the most compassionate members in the Marvel universe. When writer Chris Claremont returned to X-Men in the early 2000s, he deepened Nightcrawler’s Catholicism by making him a Catholic priest in training. The character also appears prominently in the blockbuster movie X2 (2003), where his religious identity is emphasized by the markings on his body. In a memorable exchange with Storm, Nightcrawler observes Storm’s profound anger as she says, “Anger can help one to survive.” He responds simply, “So can faith.”

Nightcrawler has resonated with many comic book lovers for generations. He doesn’t merely pontificate but is an imperfect example in the traditionally secular world of comics of how to live according to the Catholic faith. His faith doesn’t exempt him from suffering but rather provides a way to endure it with dignity and hope. And there lies the fundamental paradox of Kurt Wagner/Nightcrawler: That which appears the most demonic is the most Christlike. 

Perhaps Nightcrawler’s story offers an analogy for the experience of Christians living in an increasingly secular and atheistic world. Like him, Catholics may find themselves misunderstood, misrepresented, and even ridiculed for their beliefs. The outward signs of Catholicism can make religious conviction visible in a culture that may be hostile or dismissive of it. Like Nightcrawler, Catholics have a responsibility to meet negativity with love, forgiveness, and dignity. 

The X-Men are a chosen family united to nurture, educate, and protect one another in the face of the evil they experience in the world, with Nightcrawler being an intrinsic member in that community of mutants, exiles, and rejects. He is a character in the lineage of Quasimodo, the Elephant Man, and in a more profound sense, he recalls the lepers and outsiders encountered by Christ in the Gospels whom society considered unclean and excluded. In contrast to contemporary secular culture where people are often judged and evaluated by their outward appearance, Nightcrawler reminds us to see the world through “different eyes” and view human worth as endowed by God and the contents of their heart.
